title: Eat Your Bread in Joy
sum: Chapter 9 brings Qohelet's thinking about death to its sharpest point. The righteous and the wise are in God's hand, but no one can read from events whether God loves or hates them, because one fate comes to everyone: good and bad, clean and unclean, the worshiper and the one who stays away. The living at least know they will die; the dead know nothing, earn nothing and are forgotten (9:1–6).

Out of that bleak fact comes the book's warmest call to joy: eat your bread and drink your wine, wear white and use oil, see life with the woman you love, and do what you can with all your strength, because Sheol is coming (9:7–10). The chapter closes with a story: a poor wise man saved a small town from a great king, and no one remembered him. Wisdom is better than power, Qohelet says, but it is easily ignored (9:11–18).
readings: Read as despair

On this reading Qohelet's honesty about death leaves no room for hope. The dead know nothing, the good and the wicked meet one end, and the call to eat and drink is the sad advice of a man who sees nothing beyond the grave. Crenshaw and many critics read the chapter this way, and they point to Siduri's speech in Gilgamesh, which gives the same advice for the same reason.
Read as joy

Whybray called Qohelet a "preacher of joy". On this reading the bleak facts of 9:1–6 are there to clear away false hopes, so that the gifts of 9:7–10 can be received for what they are: God "has already" approved them. Bread, wine, clean clothes and married love are not a consolation prize but the share God gives in life.
Read in the light of later revelation

Jewish and Christian readers have usually read 9:5 and 9:10 as describing death as it looks "under the sun", from the side of this world. The Targum adds the world to come throughout, and Christian readers set the chapter beside the resurrection hope of Daniel 12:2 and the New Testament. On this reading Qohelet's limits are honest, but they are not the last word of Scripture.

views.H: The chapter's world is a small province ruled by distant kings. A great king besieging a small town (9:14) was a familiar picture in Persian and Hellenistic Judea, and the advice to enjoy food, white clothes and oil reflects the life of people with some means. The forgotten poor wise man would have struck a chord with scribes who served powerful men without credit.
views.C: Critics note the Greek and Syriac readings at 9:1–2 ("vapor" for "everything", and an extra "and the bad"), and the hard verb at 9:15, which may mean the poor man only could have saved the town. Many see 9:7–10 as one of the seven passages on enjoyment that run through the book (2:24–26; 3:12–13, 22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:7–10), each stronger than the last.
views.W: The closest ancient parallel in the whole book is Siduri's advice to Gilgamesh in the Old Babylonian epic: food, merriment, clean clothes, a washed head, a child and a wife, because the gods kept life for themselves. The Egyptian harpers' songs, sung at banquets and tombs, also urge feasting, perfume and fine linen in the face of death. Qohelet shares their realism but sets the advice under God, who gives the gifts.
views.J: The rabbis read 9:5 morally: the living are the righteous, called living even in death, and the dead are the wicked, called dead even in life (Bavli Berakhot 18a–b). They heard 9:8 as a call to repentance every day (Bavli Shabbat 153a), read the besieged town as the body attacked by the evil impulse (Bavli Nedarim 32b), and noted the clash between 9:4 and 4:2 (Bavli Shabbat 30a). The Targum turns 9:7 into God's welcome to the righteous in the world to come.
views.X: Christian readers have struggled with 9:5 and 9:10 more than with any other verses in the book. Jerome read them as true of the body, or of the dead without Christ, and Christian tradition has generally held them in tension with Jesus' teaching on the God of the living (Mark 12:27) and the hope of resurrection. Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read them as plain teaching that the dead are unconscious. Luther loved 9:7–10 as a charter for enjoying God's daily gifts with a good conscience. Some Christian allegorists saw Christ in the poor wise man who saved the town.

deep.b: For chapters 9–12 the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), with its Ketiv and Qere notes. The Greek was checked verse by verse in Rahlfs' edition and in Swete's, which prints Codex Vaticanus; the Syriac Peshitta was checked in the Leiden edition's text. No Dead Sea scroll preserves any verse of chapters 9–12: 4QQoh-a contains parts of chapters 5–7, and 4QQoh-b parts of chapter 1. Jerome's Latin, the Targum, the Talmud and the midrashim are cited from the editions and translations named in the notes.

deep.h: "The dead know nothing": 9:1–10 in Jewish and Christian reading
deep.b:
Few verses in the Old Testament have been argued over as much as 9:5 ("the dead do not know a thing") and 9:10 ("there is no doing and no reckoning, no knowledge and no wisdom in Sheol"). In context, Qohelet is comparing the living and the dead as they relate to life "under the sun": the dead have no knowledge of it, no wages from it, no memory in it and no share in it (9:5–6). Most scholars think he shared the older Israelite view of Sheol as a place of silence (Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:10–12; Psalm 115:17) and that he did not hold the hope of resurrection that appears in Daniel 12:2. He asks, after all, "Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above?" (3:21).

Jewish readers have taken several paths. The Targum adds the world to come at every turn: the dead cannot earn merit any longer, so do good now. The Talmud reads "the dead" as the wicked, dead even while alive, and "the living" as the righteous, alive even in death (Bavli Berakhot 18a–b). Medieval commentators such as Ibn Ezra read Qohelet as speaking of the body and of this world.

Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that each soul meets God at death and lives on, awaiting the resurrection (Catechism 1021–1022). They read 9:5 as speaking of the dead's part in earthly life and as a stage in revelation before Christ. Most Protestants agree: the Westminster Confession says the souls of the righteous are received into heaven at death (32.1), and Calvin wrote against the idea that souls sleep. Luther, though, spoke of the dead as "asleep" and quoted these verses, and some Lutherans and Anabaptists have taught a form of soul sleep. Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read 9:5 and 9:10 as plain teaching: death is an unconscious state until the resurrection, and these verses are among their main texts. The card on chapter 3 sets these views side by side; the card below asks a related question that 9:5–6 raises, whether the dead know of the living and whether the living may pray for them.

deep.h: What Siduri's parallel shows, and what it does not
deep.b:
The likeness between 9:7–9 and Siduri's speech in the Old Babylonian Gilgamesh is close: in both, a person who cannot escape death is told to eat and be merry, wear clean clothes, wash the head, and delight in wife and family. The order matches too. What the parallel shows is that Qohelet's advice belongs to a long tradition of ancient wisdom about death, older than Israel. What it does not show is that Qohelet copied a Babylonian tablet. The speech survives only in an Old Babylonian copy from around 1800 BC and was dropped from the later standard version, so a writer in the Persian or Hellenistic age would have known it, if at all, through a saying that had travelled on its own. Van der Toorn argues that Qohelet knew the Gilgamesh tradition; others think of a common stock of sayings, like the Egyptian harpers' songs.

The differences matter as much as the likeness. Siduri speaks as one who knows the gods have kept life for themselves; Qohelet grounds the same joys in God, who "has already" accepted them (9:7) and gives each person a "share" (9:9). Siduri's advice ends the search for eternal life; Qohelet's is set inside a book that also says God will judge (11:9; 12:14).

deep.title: Claude's theory: two kinds of forgetting
deep.b: This is my own reading, not an established one. Chapter 9 uses "forget" and "remember" twice: the dead are forgotten (9:5), and the poor wise man is not remembered (9:15). The second story may be meant as a small model of the first. The town was saved, but its savior vanished from memory as completely as the dead do, while still alive. If so, the story is not only about wisdom being ignored but about how little even good deeds secure a name under the sun, which gives extra weight to the call in 9:7–10 to take one's share now. Scholars have long noted the theme of forgetting in the book (1:11; 2:16), but I have not seen 9:5 and 9:15 read as a pair in this way.

settings.by: Qohelet, the teacher whose voice fills the book
settings.to: The book's readers, students of the wise, invited to follow his reasoning
settings.when: Part of Qohelet's long report of what he "laid on his heart" and tested; the book gives no other occasion
settings.why: Qohelet removes the comfortable idea that a person's fortune shows whether God loves or hates him. Death comes to all alike, and it ends every share in life under the sun. He wants his hearers to see the facts plainly before he tells them what to do with them (9:7–10).
settings.readers: For Jewish readers in the Persian or early Hellenistic age, when many of the wise were rethinking the old teaching that the righteous always prosper, the passage was an honest account of what they saw. Later, in Jewish reading at Sukkot, the festival of harvest joy, and in Christian reading beside the Gospel's hope of resurrection, it became a sobering reminder of mortality.
views: Qohelet denies any life beyond death and doubts that God's justice can be seen (Crenshaw, many critics).
Qohelet speaks only of life under the sun and leaves room for God's judgment, which he affirms elsewhere (3:17; 11:9) (Whybray, Bartholomew).

settings.to: The reader addressed as "you": a young or grown man with a household, bread, wine and a wife, perhaps a student or official of some means
settings.when: Following directly on the reflection on death in 9:1–6
settings.why: Because death ends everything under the sun, the hearer is told to take his God-given share now: daily food and drink, festive clothes, married love, and vigorous work. The commands are urgent, and the reason is Sheol. Knowing that they are spoken to someone who must die keeps the passage from being either hedonism or empty piety.
settings.readers: The passage became one of the book's best-loved texts. Rabbis turned 9:8 into a call to daily repentance (Bavli Shabbat 153a). Jerome had read the book in Rome with the young widow Blaesilla, to urge her to despise the world, and after her death wrote his commentary in Bethlehem (388/389) for her mother Paula and her sister Eustochium; he read such joys cautiously, while Luther and the Reformers made them a charter for receiving daily life as God's gift.

settings.what: Time and chance, and the poor wise man
settings.to: Students of wisdom and those who serve rulers
settings.when: Qohelet's further observations; the story of the besieged town is told as something he saw, though it may be a parable
settings.why: Qohelet warns the gifted that skill does not guarantee success and that wisdom, though stronger than weapons, is easily ignored, especially when it comes from the poor. For scribes and advisers who served the powerful, this was a realistic word: be wise, but do not expect to be thanked.
settings.readers: The rabbis read the story as an allegory of the soul (Bavli Nedarim 32b), and some Christians saw Christ in the forgotten savior. Modern readers often hear in it the fate of ordinary people whose good deeds history does not record.

traditions.q: "The dead do not know a thing", and they have no more share in what is done under the sun (9:5–6). Do the departed pray for the living, and may the living pray for them or ask the saints to pray? (Whether the dead are conscious at all is the question of the card on chapter 3.)
views: Yes to both. The saints in heaven intercede for the church on earth, and the living pray for the dead, especially in the Eucharist, so that those being purified may reach God (Catechism 956, 958, 1032).

Yes to both. The church on earth and the departed form one family in Christ: the faithful ask the saints and the Mother of God to pray for them, and the church prays for all the departed at every liturgy and memorial service.

The Lutheran confessions grant that the saints in heaven pray for the church in general, but reject calling on them, because Scripture gives no command or promise for it; Christ is the only mediator (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 21). On prayer for the dead, the same Apology, answering the appeal to the church fathers, says that it does not forbid such prayer, while rejecting the Mass offered for the dead (Apology 24). Lutheran practice varies: some liturgies commend the departed to God, and others avoid praying for them.

The Thirty-Nine Articles reject the "invocation of saints" as a teaching without warrant in Scripture (Article 22). Many Anglicans today pray for the departed, a practice the Prayer Book tradition has allowed in general terms.

No. Prayer is to be made "for all sorts of men living, or that shall live hereafter; but not for the dead", and worship and prayer are given to God alone, not to saints or angels (Westminster Confession 21.2, 21.4).
No. The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so they neither know of the living nor pray for them; 9:5–6 is read as plain teaching (Fundamental Belief 26).
No. The dead are conscious of nothing, as 9:5 and 9:10 say, so they cannot pray for the living or hear prayers; prayer is to Jehovah alone, through Jesus.

title: A Little Folly
sum: Chapter 10 is mostly a string of sayings, closer to Proverbs than anything else in the book. It begins with dead flies in perfume: a little folly can outweigh wisdom and honor (10:1). Then come quick sketches of the fool, who gives himself away on the road (10:2–3), and advice for a courtier when the ruler is angry: stay calm and do not walk out (10:4).

Qohelet also sees the world upside down: fools on high seats, slaves riding while princes walk (10:5–7). Every task has its risk, from digging pits to splitting logs, and wisdom is the edge that saves effort (10:8–11). The fool talks too much (10:12–15). The chapter ends with sayings about kings: woe to a land with a childish king and princes who feast at dawn, happy the land whose rulers eat to be strong, and never curse the king, even in your bedroom, for a bird will carry the news (10:16–20).
readings: Read as practical wisdom

Many readers take chapter 10 as ordinary advice for life at court and at work: be calm, be careful, sharpen your axe, watch your tongue. On this reading Qohelet is a teacher of the wise, and the chapter shows that he did not abandon wisdom even while he questioned its limits.
Read as wisdom under strain

Others notice that almost every saying shows how fragile wisdom is: one fly, one sinner, one slip of the tongue, one bad ruler can ruin it. On this reading the chapter is not a return to Proverbs but a test of it, consistent with Qohelet's conclusion that wisdom is better than folly but cannot secure anything (2:13–16).

views.H: The chapter speaks to scribes and officials who served powerful rulers: a temperamental ruler (10:4), errors from those in power (10:5), upstarts promoted (10:6–7), feasting princes (10:16–19) and a network of informers (10:20). Persian and Ptolemaic Judea had all of these. The warning not to curse the king even in private fits an empire famous for its "King's Eyes and Ears".
views.C: Critics debate how many of these sayings are Qohelet's own and how many he quotes, perhaps to disagree with them. Some see 10:2–3, 12–15 as traditional proverbs set beside Qohelet's comments (10:5–7). The text of 10:10 is among the hardest in the book, and the Greek versions differ widely there and at 10:1 and 10:17.
views.W: Many sayings have parallels in the wider wisdom tradition: the world upside down in the Egyptian Admonitions of Ipuwer, the warning about careless words in the Aramaic Words of Ahiqar, and advice on behavior at court in Egyptian instructions such as Ptahhotep's. Qohelet shares the international wisdom of the scribal class.
views.J: Jewish tradition read the snake and the "master of the tongue" (10:11) as the slanderer (Bavli Arakhin 15b) and the hours of the princes' meal as a lesson in when to eat (Bavli Shabbat 10a). The Targum applies the sayings about kings to the kings of Israel and to the righteous and wicked rulers of history.
views.X: Christian readers used chapter 10 for moral teaching: the dead flies as small sins that spoil a good name, the snake behind the wall as the devil's ambush, the right hand as the way of salvation (compare Matthew 25:33). Jerome and others applied the woe on the boy king to rulers and church leaders who lack maturity. Modern preachers often draw on 10:10 for the value of skill and preparation.

deep.b:
Chapter 10 can look like a random list, but it has threads. It begins and ends with small things that have large effects: a few dead flies (10:1) and a little bird (10:20). It moves between the fool (10:1–3, 12–15) and the ruler (10:4–7, 16–20), with the risks of ordinary work in the middle (10:8–11). And it keeps returning to speech: the fool announces his folly (10:3), the charmer's tongue is too late (10:11), the fool's lips swallow him (10:12), he multiplies words (10:14), and even a whispered curse is reported (10:20).

Qohelet's key word yitron, "gain", appears twice (10:10–11): wisdom gives the gain of success, but the charmer who is too late has no gain. That echoes the book's opening question, "What gain is there for a person in all his toil that he toils under the sun?" (1:3). Wisdom has real advantages, but only if it is used in time.

"Slaves up on horses, and princes on the ground" (10:7) is one of the oldest themes in ancient literature. Egyptian texts of the Middle Kingdom, such as the Admonitions of Ipuwer, mourn a world where the poor have become rich and officials are driven out. Proverbs says the earth shakes when a slave becomes king (Proverbs 30:22) and that it is not fitting for a slave to rule princes (Proverbs 19:10). Qohelet calls it "an evil" that comes from the ruler's mistakes (10:5). He does not say whether the fault lies with promoting the low-born or with demoting the rich, and readers have heard both a conservative complaint and a sharp comment on how arbitrary royal favor can be.

Hannah's song and Mary's song praise God for turning the world upside down in the other direction, lifting the poor and bringing down the mighty (1 Samuel 2:7–8; Luke 1:52). Qohelet's observation is cooler: under the sun, high and low change places without regard to merit.

settings.by: Qohelet, perhaps quoting traditional proverbs along with his own sayings
settings.to: Students of the wise and young men training for service, who are taught to tell the wise from the fool
settings.when: No occasion is given; this is teaching material, like the collections in Proverbs
settings.why: The sayings warn that wisdom is precious but fragile: a little folly ruins it, the fool cannot hide himself, and skill must be used in time. For students learning to serve in the households of the powerful, they gave practical rules: keep calm before an angry ruler, prepare your tools, guard your tongue.
settings.readers: Later readers used these sayings as general moral teaching; the dead flies became a picture of small sins, and the English phrase "a fly in the ointment" comes from 10:1 in the King James Version.
views: The proverbs are Qohelet's own wisdom, showing that he still valued wisdom (Whybray, Fox).
Some are traditional sayings that Qohelet quotes in order to show their limits (Gordis and others).

settings.to: A land and its people, addressed as "you, land", and the reader who lives under a king and might be tempted to curse him
settings.when: Under a monarchy; scholars think of Persian or Ptolemaic rule over Judea, when the king was far away and his officials near
settings.why: The sayings contrast a land ruined by immature, self-indulgent rulers with one blessed by noble and disciplined ones, and then warn the hearer to keep his criticism to himself, because informers are everywhere. They teach both discernment about rulers and caution in speaking of them.
settings.readers: Jewish readers in the Hellenistic age, governed from Alexandria and then Antioch, would have recognized feasting governors and royal spies. Some scholars link the "boy" king to the child-king Ptolemy V (204 BC), though most see a general saying.

title: Send Out Your Bread
sum: Chapter 11 turns uncertainty into a reason for action. "Send your bread out over the surface of the water": whether this means trade by sea, generous giving or taking risks, the point is the same. You do not know what disaster may come, so spread your efforts widely (11:1–2). Clouds rain and trees fall as they will; the farmer who waits for perfect weather never sows. You cannot know God's work any more than the path of the wind or the growth of a child in the womb, so sow in the morning and keep working in the evening (11:3–6).

Then the book's final poem begins. Light is sweet, and a long life should be enjoyed, while remembering the long darkness to come (11:7–8). Qohelet speaks directly to a young man: be glad in your youth, follow your heart and your eyes, but know that God will judge; put away frustration and trouble, for youth is vapor (11:9–10). The poem flows on into the picture of old age in chapter 12.
readings: Read as advice on risk

Many modern readers see 11:1–6 as practical guidance for living with uncertainty: invest, diversify, do not be paralyzed by what you cannot know. On this reading Qohelet is a realist who turns the limits of knowledge into a reason for bold, sensible action.
Read as a call to generosity

The Targum, Rashi and most Christian preachers read 11:1–2 as a call to give: send your bread to the poor and to many, and it will come back, in this life or the next. On this reading the chapter joins generosity to joy and judgment.
Read as a carpe diem poem

Others stress 11:7–10 as the climax of Qohelet's call to joy, close to the Latin poet Horace's "seize the day". The young man should enjoy his youth precisely because it passes. The note of judgment (11:9) keeps the joy from becoming mere pleasure-seeking.

views.H: The pictures come from an economy of farming and sea trade: grain sent by ship (Proverbs 31:14; 1 Kings 10:22), rain clouds and wind, sowing and reaping. In the Ptolemaic age, Judea was part of a busy trading world centered on Alexandria, and some scholars hear the language of commerce in 11:1–2. The address to the "young man" fits a school setting where scribes were trained.
views.C: Critics debate whether 11:9b ("But know this ... judgment") was added by an editor; most recent commentators keep it as Qohelet's own. Codex Vaticanus softens 11:9 to "walk in blameless ways", and the Greek and Syriac read "folly" for the rare word in 11:10. The poem of 11:7–12:7 is widely seen as the book's climax, structured around the words "remember" (11:8; 12:1) and "vapor" (11:8, 10; 12:8).
views.W: The Egyptian Instruction of Ankhsheshonq has a close parallel to 11:1: do a good deed and throw it in the river; when it dries, you will find it. Calls to enjoy youth before age and death are common in the harpers' songs of Egypt and in Greek lyric poetry, which scholars compare with 11:7–10.
views.J: The Targum and Rashi read 11:1 as charity, and Jewish tradition used 11:2 for giving to many. Rabbi Akiva applied 11:6 to raising new students in old age (Bavli Yevamot 62b). The rabbis were troubled by 11:9, which seemed to contradict Numbers 15:39, until they read its warning of judgment (Leviticus Rabbah 28:1).
views.X: Christian preachers have loved "Cast thy bread upon the waters" as a text on charity, often with Luke 6:38 and Galatians 6:9. Jesus' words about the wind (John 3:8) echo 11:5. The young man of 11:9 was a favorite figure in sermons to youth, and 11:3 ("where the tree falls") was long used to urge readiness for death.

deep.h: "Cast your bread": trade, charity or risk
deep.b:
Few verses in Ecclesiastes are quoted as often as 11:1, usually in the King James form, "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days." Three main readings have been offered, and they are not mutually exclusive.

Trade. "Bread" can mean grain, and sending it "over the surface of the water" suggests shipping. Solomon's ships and the merchant woman of Proverbs 31:14 bring goods "from far away". On this reading, 11:2 advises spreading cargo or investments over several ventures because no one knows which ship will sink. Some modern versions translate in this way.

Charity. The Targum reads: stretch out your bread to the poor who sail in ships, and after many days you will find its reward in the world to come. Rashi says: do good even to someone you think you will never see again. The Egyptian Instruction of Ankhsheshonq has a near twin: do a good deed and throw it in the river; when it dries, you will find it. Christian preachers took the verse this way, with Jesus' teaching to give without expecting return (Luke 6:35; Luke 14:12–14).

Risk. The surrounding verses are about acting without knowing the outcome (11:2, 4–6). On this reading 11:1 is a picture of any venture whose result lies out of sight: let go of what you have, and trust that it may return.

What all three readings share is Qohelet's main point in 11:1–6: uncertainty is no excuse for doing nothing. "Whoever keeps an eye on the wind will not sow" (11:4).

Qohelet's command to the young man, "Walk on in your heart's ways and in what your eyes see", seems to contradict the Torah, which says, "You will not go scouting after your own heart and your own eyes" (Numbers 15:39). Ancient readers felt the tension sharply. Leviticus Rabbah 28:1 says the sages wanted to withdraw the book because of it, until they read the rest of the verse: "But know this: for all of it God will bring you into judgment." Codex Vaticanus changed the line itself to "walk in blameless ways, and not in the sight of your eyes".

Modern readers divide in a similar way. Some critics think a pious editor added the warning of judgment to an originally bold call to pleasure. Others, including Fox, Seow and Whybray, think the warning is Qohelet's own and changes the meaning of the joy: enjoyment is a gift for which one will give account, so it must be the enjoyment of a person who fears God. The Jerusalem Talmud puts the same thought in its most surprising form: a person will have to give an account for every good thing he saw and did not enjoy (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:12).

echoes: Numbers 15:39; 1 Kings 10:22; Job 3:20; Job 10:21–22; Psalm 49:19; Psalm 126:5–6; Psalm 139:13–16; Proverbs 19:17; Proverbs 20:4; Proverbs 31:14; Micah 5:5; Luke 6:35; Luke 14:12–14; John 3:8; 2 Corinthians 5:10; 2 Corinthians 9:6; Galatians 6:9; 1 Timothy 6:18

settings.to: The reader as "you": someone with bread, goods and fields to manage, a householder or merchant
settings.when: No occasion is given; the sayings follow the chapter on rulers and lead into the final poem
settings.why: Qohelet has shown that no one can know the future or understand God's work. Here he draws the practical conclusion: do not freeze. Give, invest and work widely and steadily, because you cannot tell which effort will succeed. The advice is meant to free the hearer from paralysis, not to promise success.
settings.readers: Jewish and Christian readers made 11:1–2 a text on charity, and the Targum promised a reward in the world to come. Modern readers often read it as advice on risk and diversification.
views: The verses advise spreading one's ventures (many modern scholars).
The verses urge generous giving to many (Targum, Rashi, most Christian preachers).

settings.what: The final poem begins: light and youth
settings.by: Qohelet, opening the poem that runs on to 12:7
settings.to: A "young man" (11:9), a student in his prime, addressed directly as "you"
settings.when: At the end of Qohelet's teaching, as a last word to the young before the frame narrator's epilogue
settings.why: The poem urges the young man to enjoy the light while he has it, to remember his Creator before old age arrives, and to know that God will judge. It sets before him a picture of aging and death so vivid that the call to joy and to remember God becomes urgent. Knowing that it is spoken to the young explains its tone: not despair, but a wise elder's warning to those who think they have all the time in the world.
settings.readers: Jewish readers have heard the poem at Sukkot, the festival of joy, when the book is read in many synagogues. Christian monks, following Jerome, used it to call the young to renounce the world; preachers since have used it at funerals and in sermons to youth.
views: The "young man" is a pupil in a scribal school (many scholars).
The address is a literary device for every reader in youth (Fox, Longman).

title: Before the Silver Cord Is Torn
sum: The poem that began in 11:7 reaches its end. "Remember your Creator in the days of your prime," before the days of evil come (12:1). Then follows the Bible's most famous picture of old age and death: the sun and stars grow dark, the guards of the house tremble, the grinders stop, the watchers at the windows grow dark, the doors close, the almond blooms white, the caper berry fails, the mourners gather, the silver cord is torn and the golden bowl is crushed, until the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it (12:2–7). Then the motto of 1:2 returns to close Qohelet's words: "Vapor of vapors... everything is vapor" (12:8).

Then another voice speaks about Qohelet. He was wise, taught the people, weighed and arranged many proverbs, and wrote words of delight and truth (12:9–10). The words of the wise are goads and nails, given by one shepherd; beware of endless books (12:11–12). The last word: "Fear God and keep his commands," for God will judge everything, even what is hidden (12:13–14).
readings: Read as a pessimist's ending

On this reading the poem of 12:1–7 shows life collapsing into death, and 12:8 confirms that everything is vapor. The epilogue then softens or corrects Qohelet, perhaps added by an editor who wanted the book to be safe. Critics who see the book as deeply skeptical often read the ending this way.
Read as a pious ending

On this reading the epilogue states what the book has meant all along: life under the sun is vapor, so fear God, keep his commands and live in view of his judgment. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers, who took the whole book as Solomon's, and many modern evangelical commentators (Bartholomew, Longman in part) read it this way.
Read as an honest frame

Fox and others see a frame narrator who presents Qohelet's words as a wise man's bold teaching, praises him, warns students not to go further, and sets his teaching within the fear of God. The ending neither cancels Qohelet nor simply repeats him; it tells the reader how to hold a challenging book.

views.H: The images of 12:1–7 come from a well-to-do household of the Persian or Hellenistic age: guards, servants, grinding women, lattice windows, double doors onto the street, lamps of gold and silver, a well with a wheel, professional mourners. The epilogue describes the work of a scribe who weighed, studied and arranged sayings and taught the people, a picture of a teacher in a scribal school.
views.C: Scholars debate whether 12:9–14 come from one editor or two, and whether 12:13–14 were added to bring the book into line with the Torah and so help its acceptance as Scripture. The poem's text has several hard words (12:5) and a Ketiv/Qere at 12:6. Many read the poem's darkening sky as the language of the day of the LORD, applied to one person's death.
views.W: Descriptions of old age are ancient: the Egyptian Instruction of Ptahhotep opens with a lament on age (eyes dim, ears deaf, strength failing). The "house of eternity" for the tomb is Egyptian and Phoenician idiom. The epilogue's picture of a wise man who collected and arranged sayings matches the scribal culture of the whole ancient Near East.
views.J: The rabbis read 12:1–7 as an allegory of the body, part by part (Bavli Shabbat 151b–152a; Leviticus Rabbah 18:1), and heard in 12:1 "your source, your grave and your Creator". They said the book was kept in Scripture because its end is words of Torah (Bavli Shabbat 30b), and the synagogue repeats 12:13 after 12:14 so the reading ends on "Fear God". 12:11 became a classic text on the many voices of the sages coming from one God (Bavli Hagigah 3b).
views.X: Christian readers, from Jerome on, also read 12:1–7 as the body's decline, and the poem has been used at countless funerals. 12:7 was a proof text for the soul's return to God at death (Westminster Confession 32.1), while Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read it of the life-breath. Augustine took 12:13–14 as a statement of the last judgment (City of God 20.3), and the New Testament's teaching on judgment of hidden things (Romans 2:16; 1 Corinthians 4:5) was read with 12:14.

deep.h: The poem of old age: four ways to read 12:1–7
deep.b:
The poem is built on three "before" clauses (12:1, 2, 6), each beginning 'ad asher lo', "before", and ends with the dust and the spirit returning (12:7). Between them comes a cascade of images. Readers have taken them in four main ways.

1. The aging body. This is the oldest and most popular reading, found in the Targum, the Talmud (Bavli Shabbat 151b–152a), Leviticus Rabbah 18:1 and Jerome. In its usual form: the darkening sun and moon are the failing mind or sight; the guards of the house are the arms; the men of strength, the legs; the women grinding, the teeth, few now; the women at the windows, the eyes; the doors onto the street, the ears or lips; the low sound of the mill, the weak voice or poor chewing; waking at a bird's call, light sleep; the daughters of song, the failing voice or hearing; fear of heights, the old person's unsteadiness; the almond blossom, white hair; the locust weighed down, stiff hips; the caper berry, appetite and desire; the silver cord, the spine; the golden bowl, the skull; the jar and the wheel, the heart, lungs or other organs.

2. A storm. Some nineteenth-century commentators read 12:2–5 as a winter storm that darkens a house and silences its people, a picture of the gloom of age.

3. A household and a funeral. Sawyer reconstructed an original parable of a ruined estate; Fox reads the scene more literally as a great house and its town in mourning at a death, with servants trembling, work stopped, doors shut and mourners in the street.

4. The end of the world. The darkening of sun, moon and stars and the clouds returning are the language the prophets use for the day of the LORD (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10; Ezekiel 32:7–8). Seow and Fox argue that the poem uses that language for one person's death: when you die, your world ends.

The readings can work together. The body allegory explains several details (the grinders "because they are few" fits teeth perfectly), while the house and the cosmic readings explain the poem's mood. Most commentators now think Qohelet layered his images rather than writing a code to be decoded line by line.

deep.h: "The spirit goes back to God, who gave it" (12:7)
deep.b:
12:7 reverses the creation of Genesis 2:7: God formed the man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life; now the dust goes back to the earth (Genesis 3:19) and the ruach to God. Psalm 104:29–30 and Job 34:14–15 say the same: when God takes back his breath, creatures die and return to dust.

The question is what the ruach is. In 3:19–21 Qohelet used the same word for the life-breath that humans share with animals, and asked whether anyone knows if the human spirit goes up. Here he states that it returns to God, without saying whether it returns as a conscious self. Many scholars think Qohelet means the life-breath lent by God, which goes back to its giver, with no claim about personal survival. Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read the verse this way: the spirit is the life-force, not a conscious soul. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant teaching reads it, in the light of the New Testament, as the soul returning to God at death to await the resurrection; the Westminster Confession echoes the verse directly (32.1). Jewish tradition took the verse both ways and drew a moral from it: give the soul back to God as pure as he gave it (Bavli Shabbat 152b). Whatever one decides, the verse ends the poem not with the grave but with God.

deep.h: The epilogue (12:9–14): one editor or two?
deep.b:
From 12:9 the book speaks about Qohelet, not as Qohelet. This voice was heard at the start (1:1–2) and once in the middle ("says Qohelet", 7:27). Who is it?

Two editors. Many critical scholars hear two hands. The first (12:9–11) admires Qohelet: he was wise, taught the people, weighed and arranged proverbs, wrote honest words of delight; the words of the wise are goads and nails from one shepherd. The second (12:12–14) is more cautious: beware of anything beyond these, books are endless, and the whole matter comes down to fearing God and keeping the commandments, because God will judge. On this view the second editor wanted to make Qohelet safe for readers of the Torah.

One frame narrator. Fox argued that the same voice speaks in 1:1–2, 7:27 and 12:8–14: the author himself, who created Qohelet as a character and frames his words, at once praising them and setting them within the fear of God. On this view the epilogue is not a correction but part of the book's design, like the prose frame of Job.

A canonical conclusion. Sheppard argued that 12:13–14 read Qohelet in the light of the Torah, as Ben Sira does with wisdom (Sirach 24:23), and so mark the book as Scripture for those who follow the commandments. The rabbis seem to have read it so: the book was kept because its end is words of Torah (Bavli Shabbat 30b).

Whatever its origin, the epilogue tells the reader how to take the book: as the work of a wise and honest teacher, whose sayings prod like goads, to be read within the fear of God. On how book.json presents the frame narrator and the book's acceptance into Scripture, see the book's opening pages.

The epilogue's last word joins two phrases. "Fear God" is Qohelet's own (3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12–13): before a God whose ways cannot be traced, the right response is reverent awe. "Keep his commands" is the language of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 6:2; Deuteronomy 10:12–13), which Qohelet had not used. Together they make the book's end sound like Proverbs 1:7 and Job 28:28: the fear of the LORD is the beginning and the sum of wisdom.

"For this is the whole of being human" is famously compressed. The KJV's "the whole duty of man" added "duty". Rabbi Elazar said the whole world was created only for the one who fears God (Bavli Berakhot 6b), and Augustine read "this is every man" (City of God 20.3). The final verse promises judgment on everything done and hidden, good or evil, which the New Testament applies to the last judgment (Romans 2:16; 2 Corinthians 5:10). In the synagogue, 12:13 is read again after 12:14 so that the book ends with the command to fear God rather than the word "evil".

settings.what: Remember your Creator: the poem of old age
settings.by: Qohelet, finishing the poem begun at 11:7; the closing motto (12:8) is given by the frame narrator, "says Qohelet"
settings.to: The "young man" of 11:9, still addressed as "you" ("your Creator", "your prime")
settings.when: The end of Qohelet's teaching; the poem looks ahead to the hearer's own old age and death
settings.why: The poem gives the young man a reason to remember God now: a picture of decline so vivid that he cannot think he has endless time. Every image, whether of a failing body, a house in mourning or a darkening world, ends at the grave and the return of the spirit to God. Because it is spoken to someone young, it is a warning and an invitation, not a lament.
settings.readers: The rabbis and Jerome read it line by line as the aging body (Bavli Shabbat 151b–152a; Leviticus Rabbah 18:1). Christian monks used it to call novices to leave the world early; preachers have read it at funerals for centuries, and modern readers often meet it in the King James wording ("or ever the silver cord be loosed").

settings.by: The frame narrator, a voice that speaks about Qohelet in the third person (as in 1:1–2 and 7:27), perhaps the author himself or one or two later editors
settings.to: "My son" (12:12): a student of the wise, and through him every reader of the book
settings.when: After Qohelet's last words (12:8), as a closing word on the man and his book; the date is debated, from the book's own time (Persian or early Hellenistic Judea) to the time when the book was being received as Scripture
settings.why: The epilogue tells the student how to receive Qohelet: he was wise, honest and careful, and his sayings are meant to prod like goads and hold like nails, but the student should not go wandering beyond them into endless books. Its final word names the whole of being human: fear God and keep his commands, because God will judge everything. Knowing that it speaks to a student explains its tone: it is a teacher's advice on how to read a challenging book.
settings.readers: The epilogue helped the book find its place in Scripture: the rabbis said it was kept because its end is words of Torah (Bavli Shabbat 30b). Jews read the whole book at Sukkot in many communities, repeating 12:13 at the end. Christian readers from Jerome to the Puritans quoted 12:13–14 as the summary of the book and of true religion.
views: The author speaks in his own voice in 1:1–2, 7:27 and 12:8–14 (Fox).
12:9–11 and 12:12–14 come from two hands, the second more cautious (many critical scholars).
12:13–14 tie the book to the Torah and mark its place in Scripture (Sheppard).
Traditional Jewish and Christian readers took the epilogue as Solomon's own last word.
